record.reply: Both Ben and Cara possess the same urgent basic survival need, so attentiveness and responsibility place them on an equal footing at the first two phases of care.  The decisive difference arises at the third phase—competence.  Giving the dose to Ben delivers a 95 % chance of meeting that urgent need, whereas giving it to Cara delivers only 5 %.  When two equally urgent needs compete for a single resource that can help only one person, Tronto’s competence phase instructs the carer to use the resource effectively.  Promise-based trust is a genuine fourth-phase (responsiveness) consideration, but care ethics does not license a response that is known to be dramatically ineffective at meeting the very need the promise concerns.  Honouring the promise therefore cannot override the huge competence gap, because keeping a promise that predictably fails the underlying caring purpose undercuts the integrity of care itself. record.framework_commitment: Attentiveness and responsibility treat both patients’ survival as equally weighty; competence then requires using the scarce medicine where it is vastly more effective, and responsiveness (promise-keeping) cannot justify knowingly incompetent care.
record.reasoning_bridge: Effectiveness is drawn from stated probabilities (PROP:WORLD:E2 vs. PROP:WORLD:E4).  Promise is drawn from PROP:WORLD:RECOGNITION:4697fd89cd506cc4.  Care ethics ranks phases sequentially; a severe failure at competence blocks a later-phase consideration from overriding it.
record.remaining_uncertainty: If Cara’s survival probability were comparable to Ben’s, or if further relational duties toward Cara were established (e.g., long-standing caregiver relationship), the priority might reverse.
record.reversal_condition: Cara’s survival chance rises to near Ben’s (≈ 90 %), or additional entrusted relationship uniquely binds Ada to Cara.
